subject: Chemistry
title: The Polar C–X Bond: Polarity, Bond Length and Strength
summary: The C–X bond is polar: the halogen pulls the shared pair, so carbon is δ+ and the halogen δ−, and nucleophiles attack that carbon. From F to I the halogen gets bigger, so the C–X bond gets longer (139 → 214 pm) and weaker (452 → 234 kJ mol⁻¹). That is why R–I reacts fastest and R–F slowest, even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen; and why CH₃Cl, not CH₃F, has the largest dipole moment (μ = q × d).

notes.title: 06 – The Polar C–X Bond
notes.blurb: polarity, bond length, bond enthalpy, dipole moment and reactivity, with NCERT data

keyPoints: The C–X bond is **polar**: X is more electronegative than C, so carbon is **δ+** and the halogen **δ−**.
Nucleophiles (OH⁻, CN⁻, RO⁻) attack the **δ+ carbon** and push out X⁻.
From F to I the halogen gets bigger: **bond length increases** (139, 178, 193, 214 pm).
Longer bond, poorer overlap: **bond enthalpy decreases** (452, 351, 293, 234 kJ mol⁻¹).
μ = q × d, so the largest dipole is **CH₃Cl** (1.860 D) > CH₃F > CH₃Br > CH₃I.
Reactivity towards nucleophiles: **R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F**: the weakest bond breaks first.

sections.h: Polarity: a tug of war for the shared pair

blocks.p: In a haloalkane the halogen X is bonded to an sp³ carbon by one shared pair. Every halogen is **more electronegative than carbon**, so it pulls the shared pair towards itself. Carbon becomes **δ+** and the halogen **δ−**: the C–X bond is a **polar bond**.
**Why it matters:** the δ+ carbon is the target of every nucleophile (OH⁻, CN⁻, RO⁻). The nucleophile attacks it and X leaves as X⁻: the start of nucleophilic substitution, SN1, SN2 and elimination.

sections.h: Size, bond length and bond strength

blocks.p: Down group 17 the halogen atom gets **bigger**, so the C–X bond gets **longer**. A bigger halogen overlaps less well with carbon, and a longer bond is a **weaker** bond, so the bond enthalpy falls.

Fluorine carries the biggest partial charge, but the C–F bond is very short. Chlorine's charge is a little smaller, but its bond is much longer, so the product is largest for **CH₃Cl**: CH₃Cl > CH₃F > CH₃Br > CH₃I.
All four C–X bonds are polar, so the nucleophile is attracted in every case. But X can only leave if the **C–X bond breaks**, and the weakest bond breaks fastest. So, for the same alkyl group:
**Takeaway:** polarity invites the nucleophile; bond strength decides how easily the halogen leaves. From F to I: bond longer, bond weaker, reactivity higher.

list: “C–F is the most reactive because F is the most electronegative.” It is the least reactive: C–F is the strongest bond.
“CH₃F has the largest dipole moment.” It is CH₃Cl, because μ depends on distance as well as charge.
“Bond length falls down the group.” It rises, 139 → 214 pm.
